summary: Defines a flexible way to support Differentiated Services over MPLS networks. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Some data deserves faster treatment. This shows how to give priority levels to traffic traveling on labeled network paths.

questions: what is an e-lsp in mpls
what is the difference between e-lsp and l-lsp
how does diffserv work over mpls
subtitle: How to carry Differentiated Services traffic classes across MPLS label switched paths, with two LSP flavors to choose from.

tldr.problem: Diff-Serv routers read a code point in the IP header to decide how to treat each packet, but MPLS routers forward on labels and may not see that header. Operators also want freedom in how traffic classes map onto label switched paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two kinds of LSP. An E-LSP carries up to eight behavior aggregates and uses the 3-bit EXP field in the MPLS shim header to pick the treatment. An L-LSP carries one ordered aggregate, with the scheduling class implied by the label itself. RSVP and LDP extensions signal which kind is wanted.
tldr.outcome: Operators can put all classes on one LSP, or give each class its own LSP, to suit their traffic engineering and protection goals. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3032 and is itself updated by RFC 5462.

today: RFC 3270 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3032 and is itself updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: Diff-Serv Meets MPLS
sections.content:
In a Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) domain, packets that need the same treatment form a Behavior Aggregate (BA). The ingress node marks each packet with a Diff-Serv Code Point (DSCP), and every node along the way uses it to choose a Per Hop Behavior (PHB), which sets the scheduling treatment and, in some cases, the drop probability.

In an MPLS network, a Label Switched Path (LSP) is set up with signaling, and each Label Switch Router (LSR) forwards a packet by its label. Because the IP header may not be visible to an LSR, the way it learns and applies the PHB has to differ from a normal Diff-Serv router.

This RFC gives a flexible solution for the PHBs defined at the time (the Default, Class Selector, Assured Forwarding and Expedited Forwarding groups) and leaves room for future ones. It covers IPv4 and IPv6 and describes unicast operation only; multicast is left for future study. The administrator decides how BAs are spread over LSPs, which also lets different classes get different levels of MPLS protection.
sections.eli5: Imagine a highway where each car has a sticker saying how important it is. The road crew needs a way to read that sticker even when the car is wearing a new cover. This RFC says how.

sections.title: E-LSPs and L-LSPs
sections.content:
An EXP-Inferred-PSC LSP (E-LSP) can carry one or more Ordered Aggregates, up to eight BAs for a given FEC. The EXP field of the MPLS shim header tells the LSR the full PHB, meaning both the PHB Scheduling Class (PSC) and the drop precedence. The EXP-to-PHB mapping is either signaled when the label is set up or taken from a preconfigured mapping.

A Label-Only-Inferred-PSC LSP (L-LSP) carries a single Ordered Aggregate for one FEC. The PSC is signaled at label setup, so the LSR infers it from the label alone. The drop precedence travels in the EXP field when a shim header is used, or in a link-layer field such as ATM CLP when it is not.

For a given FEC, any mix of zero or more E-LSPs and zero or more L-LSPs is allowed unless the link type restricts it. When several LSPs carry the same OA, for example to share load, all packets of one microflow MUST use the same LSP, and each LSP MUST be able to carry all the active BAs of its OA. Either kind may be set up with or without bandwidth reservation; a reservation does not require per-LSP scheduling, because treatment is still applied per BA.
sections.eli5: An E-LSP is one lane where every car carries a sticker for its priority. An L-LSP is a lane that is only for one priority, so you can tell from the lane alone.

sections.title: The Four-Stage Forwarding Model
sections.content:
The RFC models a Diff-Serv LSR as four stages. (A) Incoming PHB determination finds which BA a packet belongs to. (B) Outgoing PHB determination is an optional traffic conditioning step that may demote or promote the packet, so the outgoing PHB can differ from the incoming one. (C) Label forwarding picks the next hop. (D) Encoding writes the Diff-Serv information into the EXP field, ATM CLP, Frame Relay DE or 802.1 User_Priority. The model describes behavior and does not constrain an implementation.

Each label carries a Diff-Serv Context: the LSP type (E-LSP or L-LSP), the supported PHBs, an Encaps-to-PHB mapping for incoming labels and a set of PHB-to-Encaps mappings for outgoing labels. The context is stored in the Incoming Label Map for each incoming label and in the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry for each outgoing label.

If a label maps to several next-hop entries, the LSR MUST choose one whose context supports the outgoing PHB of the packet.
sections.eli5: A packet comes in, the router reads its sticker, maybe changes it, sends it on its way, and writes a fresh sticker for the next stop.

sections.title: Tunneling Models
sections.content:
An LSP is a kind of tunnel, so the RFC adapts the models from RFC 2983. Intermediate nodes see only the outer Diff-Serv information, which can change along the path. Unlike IP tunnels, LSPs generally have no behavior analogous to Penultimate Hop Popping unless PHP is used, and PHP hides the outer information from the egress.

  • Pipe Model (MUST be supported): the LSP hides its intermediate nodes. The egress applies its PHB from the outer (LSP) information, then pops. It therefore works only without PHP.
  • Short Pipe Model (MAY be supported): the egress applies its treatment from the tunneled (inner) information, so it can also work with PHP.
  • Uniform Model (MAY be supported): there is exactly one meaningful piece of Diff-Serv information, always in the outermost label entry. MPLS is transparent to Diff-Serv.

LSR behavior differs between the models only on push and pop. Tunnels can nest to any depth, and the ingress and the popping LSR of a level must use the same model, while different levels may use different models.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the sticker inside the box matters, sometimes only the sticker on the outside. The three models are three rules for which sticker counts.

sections.title: Mapping PHBs to Header Bits
sections.content:
For an incoming E-LSP the LSR looks up the EXP value in an EXP-to-PHB table. That table is signaled, or is the preconfigured one. LSRs MUST allow local configuration of the preconfigured mapping, which must be consistent across the domain or remarked as needed. If none has been configured, the LSR should use a default that maps all EXP values to the Default PHB. For an outgoing E-LSP a PHB-to-EXP mapping is required, and extra PHB-to-CLP, DE or 802.1 mappings apply when the LSP leaves over ATM, Frame Relay or a LAN with several 802.1 traffic classes.

For L-LSPs the mappings depend on the PSC. The mandatory shim-header mapping is shown in the table. Over ATM and Frame Relay only one bit (CLP or DE) carries drop precedence, so AFn1 maps to 0 while AFn2 and AFn3 map to 1.

Merging is restricted. E-LSPs can be merged only if they support exactly the same set of BAs, and L-LSPs only if they support the same PSC. LSRs MUST check this at label setup, and the bandwidth downstream of an L-LSP merge must carry the sum of the merged traffic, which matters especially for EF.
sections.eli5: There is a small lookup card that says which bits on the packet mean which priority. Both ends of a link must use the same card.

sections.title: Signaling with RSVP and LDP
sections.content:
Two signaling protocols get extensions. For RSVP, a new optional DIFFSERV object (class 65) goes in Path messages for LSP tunnels. C-Type 1 is for an E-LSP and C-Type 2 is for an L-LSP, which carries a 16-bit PSC. For LDP, a new optional Diff-Serv TLV (type 0x0901) rides in Label Request, Label Mapping and Notification messages, with a T bit of 0 for an E-LSP and 1 for an L-LSP.

An E-LSP is signaled with no object, or one with no MAP entries, to mean the preconfigured mapping. A signaled mapping has one 32-bit MAP entry per EXP value, up to eight, each holding a 3-bit EXP and a 16-bit PHBID. An L-LSP always carries its PSC. LSRs that support signaled E-LSPs or L-LSPs MUST support the object or TLV; support is optional for preconfigured-mapping E-LSPs.

RSVP error code 27 is Diff-Serv Error, with values 1 to 5: Unexpected DIFFSERV object, Unsupported PHB, Invalid EXP-PHB mapping, Unsupported PSC and Per-LSP context allocation failure. LDP has five matching status codes. A mapping is invalid if a value appears twice or the PHBID encoding is wrong. If a path set-up fails for an unknown object, the sender should consider falling back to E-LSPs with the preconfigured mapping.
sections.eli5: Routers ask each other to build a lane by sending a note. The note says either 'use the usual card' or 'here is a custom card' or 'this lane is only for one priority'. If a router cannot do it, it sends back an error.

sections.title: Link Types: PPP, LAN, ATM and Frame Relay
sections.content:
On PPP, LAN, and non-label-controlled ATM and Frame Relay interfaces, any mix of E-LSPs and L-LSPs per FEC is allowed. A Diff-Serv LSR MUST support E-LSPs with the preconfigured mapping there, and MAY support signaled E-LSPs and L-LSPs.

On label switching controlled ATM (LC-ATM) and Frame Relay (LC-FR) interfaces, E-LSPs are not supported, so only L-LSPs are used and an LSR MUST support them. The RFC does not choose ATM service categories or Frame Relay parameters; it only requires that the forwarding behavior comply with the relevant PHB specifications. On ATM, frame discard mechanisms such as Early Packet Discard SHOULD be enabled for all PHBs described. It assumes shim header encapsulation on ATM and generic encapsulation on Frame Relay.
sections.eli5: Some roads only have single-purpose lanes. On those, you must use the one-priority-per-lane kind.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security section is a single statement: the document does not introduce any new security issues beyond those inherent in Diff-Serv, MPLS and RSVP, and may use the same mechanisms proposed for those technologies.

IANA considerations cover the allocations made by this RFC: class number 65 for the RSVP DIFFSERV object, RSVP error code 27 for Diff-Serv Error with values 1 through 5, a new LDP TLV number, and five new LDP status codes. Future values for the RSVP error field are handled First Come First Served.
sections.eli5: The authors say this adds no new dangers of its own, and they list the new numbers they registered.
